title: Css mastery — Module Quiz
description: Mixed quiz covering all topics in Css mastery.

questions.question: Flexbox is best for which kind of layout?

options.text: One-dimensional (a single row OR column) alignment
Two-dimensional grid layouts with rows AND columns

questions.explanation: Flexbox is one-dimensional (main axis only). For 2D row+column layouts, CSS Grid is the better tool.

questions.question: justify-content controls alignment along the:

options.text: Main axis (the direction set by flex-direction)

questions.explanation: justify-content = main-axis distribution (start/center/space-between...). align-items = cross-axis.

questions.question: To vertically AND horizontally center a single child you use:
questions.explanation: Flex centering needs both axes: justify-content (main) + align-items (cross). This is the classic centering trick.

questions.question: flex: 1 is shorthand for:
questions.explanation: flex:1 = grow 1, shrink 1, basis 0% — items share free space equally. A common equal-width pattern.

questions.question: flex-basis defines:

options.text: The initial main-size of an item before grow/shrink is applied

questions.explanation: flex-basis sets the starting size along the main axis; grow/shrink then adjust it relative to free space.

questions.question: To prevent a flex item from shrinking below its content you set:
questions.explanation: flex-shrink:0 stops the item from shrinking. Useful for icons/buttons you want to keep at natural size.

questions.question: flex-wrap: wrap allows items to:

options.text: Flow onto multiple lines when they don't fit

questions.explanation: wrap lets flex items break to new lines instead of overflowing; align-content then controls spacing of those lines.

questions.question: A common mistake is:

options.text: Using flexbox for full 2D page grids instead of CSS Grid

questions.explanation: Flexbox is 1D; forcing it into complex 2D layouts gets awkward. Reach for Grid for 2D, flex for 1D alignment.

questions.question: CSS Grid is primarily used for:
questions.explanation: Grid excels at 2D layouts; Flexbox is for 1D. Choose based on whether you need row+column control.

questions.question: grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(200px, 1fr)) does what?

options.text: Creates as many 200px-min columns as fit, stretching them to fill (responsive)
Sets a fixed 200px width regardless of screen

questions.explanation: auto-fit + minmax is the classic responsive grid: columns auto-flow to fill width, each at least 200px.

questions.question: The 'fr' unit represents:

options.text: A fraction of the available grid space

questions.explanation: 1fr = one share of leftover space. Used to distribute tracks proportionally after fixed sizes are accounted for.

questions.question: To place an item in a specific area you can use:
questions.explanation: Grid items are placed via line-based (grid-column: 1 / 3) or named areas (grid-template-areas).

questions.question: gap in grid controls:

options.text: The spacing between rows and columns

questions.explanation: gap (row-gap/column-gap) sets gutters between tracks without margins — cleaner than margin hacks.

questions.question: grid-template-areas lets you:

options.text: Name regions in a visual ASCII-like layout and assign items to them

questions.explanation: grid-template-areas uses named cells ('header header' / 'sidebar main') for intuitive, readable layouts.

questions.question: Which is TRUE about Grid vs Flexbox?
questions.explanation: The key mental model: Grid = 2D (both axes at once), Flex = 1D (content-driven along one axis).

questions.question: justify-items vs justify-content in grid differ because:

options.text: justify-items aligns items INSIDE their cells; justify-content aligns the grid TRACKS in the container

questions.explanation: justify-items positions items within their grid area; justify-content positions the whole grid when it's narrower than the container.

questions.question: position: absolute removes an element from normal flow and positions it relative to:

options.text: Its nearest positioned ancestor (or the viewport if none)

questions.explanation: absolute is offset from the nearest ancestor with position != static. Without one, it falls back to the initial containing block (viewport).

questions.question: position: fixed differs from absolute because it is relative to:
questions.explanation: fixed positions relative to the viewport and doesn't move on scroll (great for headers/modals).

questions.question: position: sticky behaves like:

options.text: relative until it would scroll past a threshold, then sticks like fixed within its parent

questions.explanation: sticky toggles between relative and fixed based on scroll position, constrained to its containing block — perfect for sticky headers.

questions.question: For position: absolute/relative/fixed, the offsets (top/right/bottom/left) are ignored when:
questions.explanation: top/left/etc. only apply to positioned elements (relative/absolute/fixed/sticky). With static they're ignored.

questions.question: z-index controls:

options.text: Stacking order of positioned elements (which appears on top)

questions.explanation: z-index sets paint order among positioned elements within the same stacking context; higher = closer to viewer.

questions.question: A 'stacking context' is created by, among others:

options.text: position + z-index, opacity < 1, transform, will-change, flex/grid child with z-index

questions.explanation: Many properties create a new stacking context (transform, opacity, position+z-index, will-change...), scoping z-index locally.

questions.question: To center an absolutely-positioned box both ways you use:
questions.explanation: Offset to 50% then translate back by half its own size — the classic absolute-centering technique.

questions.question: When is absolute positioning a poor choice?

options.text: For whole page layout (it breaks document flow and responsive behavior)

questions.explanation: Absolute positioning yanks elements from flow; using it for major layouts harms responsiveness. Flex/Grid are better for layout.

questions.question: Which selector matches a <button> element with class 'primary'?
questions.explanation: button.primary = element type AND class. .primary button (descendant) and button#primary (ID) are different.

questions.question: The child combinator '>' selects:
questions.explanation: ul > li matches li's that are direct children of ul. The space (descendant) combinator matches any depth.

questions.question: a:hover, a:focus, a:active are examples of:
questions.explanation: Pseudo-classes (:hover, :focus, :nth-child) target states/positions. Pseudo-elements (::before) target parts of an element.

questions.question: input[type="text"] is an:
questions.explanation: Square brackets denote attribute selectors; they match elements by attribute presence/value.

questions.question: p::first-line targets:

options.text: The first formatted line of a paragraph (a pseudo-element)

questions.explanation: ::first-line (double-colon) is a pseudo-element styling the first line. ::first-letter targets the first character.

questions.question: The universal selector is written as:
questions.explanation: * matches any element. It has the lowest specificity (0,0,0,0) and is often used in resets (e.g. * { box-sizing }).
